19.name: An Cnoc Ruadh
19.history: An Cnoc Ruadh stood above the western end of Loch chrom, a palisaded hall over salt-pans and boats, held by a line older than the king's crowning. Beathag Ruadh held it when the valleys came in to the king and did not come; Uisdean Mòr cut the ditch across the neck, and saw his palisade burned twice, and at last knelt in the ford to put his hands between the king's in the two hundred and ninetieth year. Seonag weighed the salt tallies before the king with a pebble bag; Murchadh Gearr walked Rathad an t-Salainn every autumn; Lachlann Ruadh took Eilidh Ghlas's younger son to foster and was called Lachlann an Altraim for it. Peigi Dhubh laid the stone landing at the river-mouth, and the harbour grew round it. The hill traded salt for Dùn ìseal's wool at the ford fourteen miles off, and its reciters kept their own roll, from Beathag Ruadh to Seumas Òg, which was spoken whole at the ford only once.
19.known_for: salt, the palisade, and the fosterling

16.history: A harbour of Seann-Dhaoine on the far north-west coast, with a tower on its point older than any telling. The hill-folk who came there kept Seann-Dhaoine' name for it and a watch in the tower. In the two thousand four hundred and twenty-first year four watchers saw a long back rise off the point in the failing light and go under without a sound; that season the wrack south of the tower gave up stitched planks from hulls built for open water, and no household would claim them. Micheil Beag laid the planks against his wall, and Anndra Breac, a teller of that shore, made from them a telling of a crossing that he carried to the ford and was shouted down for. He was last seen walking south along the strand below the tower.
16.known_for: the tower's watch and the stitched planks

431.history: A harbour of Seann-Dhaoine on the southern coast, empty through the first two thousand years of the age and taken up again by fishing households in the long settling. Within a few generations of its resettling it was the busiest quay on that coast, boats going out on every tide and its hook-makers at work from first light beating out bone hooks faster than the fishing could wear them. The tale of the grey stranger who lifted the boulder at Ceann leathan grew hands like a smith's iron at a fire near here, an embellishment Alasdair Làidir spent the rest of his life correcting, and an old woman of this shore carried her own telling of the stone to the ford.
431.known_for: the busiest quay of the south

18.history: A town of Seann-Dhaoine on the Abhainn chaol a little above the river mouth, on footings no hill-folk laid. Its middens were Seann-Dhaoine' own, and its tally stones, each cut with a single stroke, stood upright in them. The hill-folk who came after them built along the middens' shoulder. In the four thousand three hundred and sixty-sixth year a family digging a house-floor struck a row of the tally stones, knew them for what they were, and set them back as they lay rather than break them; a year later the last of Seann-Dhaoine' middens here was disturbed, and the households closed it again.

297.history: A long ridge in the south between the valleys and the coast, where households settled in the middle centuries within an earth bank. It dug and lined a well inside its own earthwork in the two thousand four hundred and sixty-seventh year so that its water-carriers need not go down to the shore while a storm still had teeth in it, and the town was taken up in earnest a generation later. It traded south to the coast and north to the ford, and sent its people to An Cruinneachadh Mòr in the three thousandth year. Its households kept the handful by the cup and the sharing by the count of mouths, and in the lean years they opened their store within the bank to the coast below them as Dùn ìseal had opened its own.

363.history: A harbour on the south-eastern shore below Làrach an Dùin, the ruin of the old builders, settled by fishing households in the three thousand and twenty-eighth year. They built their houses with doors to the sea and backs to the broken walls, and would not go up to the ruin or carry off its dressed stone lying loose for the taking; an old woman of that shore said a wall raised by other hands keeps its own quarrel. The contests below Clachan nan Gaoth at Ceann leathan drew its young men every autumn, and it was a son of this shore's herders, Alasdair Làidir, who threw every man who stood against him at three-and-twenty.
